title: Katzmann: Canons and the limits of interpretive rules (pp. 50–54)
shortTitle: Katzmann: Canons and the limits of interpretive rules (pp. 50–54)
summary: Katzmann accepts the usefulness of some canons but argues that competing rules, uneven drafting practices, and substantive presumptions limit their determinacy.
notes:
The reading distinguishes interpretive conventions about semantics, grammar, and context from presumptions governing institutional arrangements and private rights. Examples include giving words significance, associated-word inferences, disfavoring implied repeal, constitutional avoidance, sovereign-immunity rules, and lenity. Scalia and Garner defend valid canons as stabilizing interpretation but acknowledge that one canon may yield to stronger principles.

Katzmann emphasizes the absence of a universal ranking system and the discretion required to identify absurdity or select among competing conventions. He also asks whether the rules match legislative drafting: staff may use associated-word reasoning without knowing its Latin name while remaining unaware of some clear-statement rules. A new judicial presumption can change the effect of legislation drafted against an older background. He therefore favors canons as context-sensitive aids alongside reliable legislative materials, rather than assuming they eliminate judgment. His suggested hierarchy of legislative history gives greater weight to conference and committee reports, then informed bill-manager statements, with stray uninvolved floor statements carrying less.
